picks.title: Topological Multicomponent Superconductivity with Sizable s -Wave Admixture in Twisted Bilayer Cuprates
picks.abstract: We investigate multicomponent superconductivity in twisted bilayer cuprates with order parameter s + d 1 e i ϕ 1 + d 2 e i ϕ 2 , where s = s 1 + s 2 is the layer-symmetric s -wave pairing and d i is the d -wave pairing in layer i . When ϕ 1 − ϕ 2 ≠ 0 , π , this three-component state spontaneously breaks time-reversal and C 4 rotational symmetries and can realize a topologically nontrivial phase. Ginzburg-Landau analysis and self-consistent mean-field calculations show that this state is stabilized over a broad parameter regime. We further identify nematic Kerr anisotropy as a key signature distinguishing it from s + i d and d 1 + e i ϕ d 2 , and find that its Josephson critical current remains sizable near the 45 ∘ twist. Our results show that s -wave pairing does not preclude chiral topological superconductivity, pointing to twisted cuprates as a more robust platform than previously appreciated.

picks.title: Nonperturbative constraints on stability and renormalization group flows in nonequilibrium matter
picks.abstract: We derive constraints on renormalization group (RG) flows and stability of phases in nonequilibrium systems using quantum information inequalities. These constraints involve conditional mutual information (CMI), which quantifies correlations between spatially separated regions not mediated by their surroundings. First, assuming CMI is UV finite, we derive a monotonicity constraint on its crossover scaling function. Under certain assumptions, this implies that the CMI scaling exponent cannot increase along the RG flow. Second, we bound the CMI of a convex mixture of states in terms of the CMI of individual components. We use this inequality to infer perturbative stability of spontaneous symmetry breaking states against quantum channels that explicitly break symmetry. We illustrate these constraints through several examples, including decoherence-driven transitions in classical symmetry-broken states, area-law CMI in anisotropic conserved dynamics, and even transitions in pure quantum states. We also discuss implications for classical nonequilibrium steady states.

picks.title: Detection and Statistics of Large-scale Sector Boundary Crossings in the Solar Wind: The SBCross Catalog
picks.abstract: Heliospheric sector boundary crossings (SBCs), composed of the heliospheric current sheet (HCS), heliospheric plasma sheet (HPS), and surrounding plasma halo, represent fundamental structures in the solar wind that influence interplanetary dynamics and space weather. We present the SBCross catalog, an automated, publicly available database containing 1076 SBC events derived from in situ observations spanning more than 30 yr (1995–2026), covering Solar Cycles 23 and 24 alongside the rising and maximum phases of Solar Cycle 25. By combining interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) and 255 eV suprathermal electron pitch angle distribution (PAD) data, our algorithm reliably captures large-scale polarity transitions, with 76% of detected SBCs exhibiting clear HPS signatures ( β > 1, n peak > 10 cm −3 ). Across the catalog, we find an average occurrence rate of ≈2.6 events per Carrington rotation, a median event duration of ≈9.0 hr, and a median physical thickness of ≈7.4 × 10 6 km. Furthermore, approximately ≈15% of detected SBCs interact with interplanetary coronal mass ejections (CMEs), with this proportion rising up to 33% during solar maximum. These CME-associated events exhibit systematically longer durations (median of 10.0 hr), 54% larger physical thicknesses, and higher average solar wind velocities. Notably, all high-velocity SBC events (>600 km s −1 ) are exclusively driven by CME interactions, demonstrating local plasma pileup and structural entanglement resulting from fast CMEs overtaking the ambient slow background. The SBCross catalog serves as an updated successor to the classic SBC list by L. Svalgaard, delivering a standardized, open-access resource for the heliophysics community to systematically investigate sector boundary transitions.

picks.title: Are Nucleosynthetic Yields Universal? Interpreting the Multielemental Abundances of Quiescent Galaxies over Cosmic Time Using Milky Way Stars
picks.abstract: The detailed abundance patterns of quiescent galaxies offer powerful constraints on their formation and evolution. Yet physical insight remains elusive, as nucleosynthetic yields are notoriously uncertain. We introduce a framework that circumvents this problem by using Milky Way abundance trends as empirical proxies for initial mass function (IMF)-averaged yields. Applied to quiescent galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey ( z ∼ 0), LEGA-C ( z ∼ 0.7), and JWST/SUSPENSE ( z ∼ 2), our approach recovers the α - and Fe-peak abundances with a median offset of ∼0.05 dex across 10 elements, compared to ∼0.23 dex for theoretical yields. Systematic residuals of up to ∼0.1–0.2 dex remain for some elements in galaxies with the highest velocity dispersions. The largest discrepancies arise in N, Sr, Ba, and (at z ∼ 2) C, all of which depend on asymptotic giant branch enrichment, a channel we do not explicitly model. We explore the impact of a top-heavy IMF and find that it can shift the IMF-averaged core-collapse supernova yields by ∼0.05–0.2 dex in a direction that reduces the systematic residuals. Surprisingly, the predictions succeed without modeling the full chemical-evolution history of a galaxy: Mg and Fe alone are sufficient to predict the remaining α - and Fe-peak elements. Combined with previous results in dwarf galaxies and the Milky Way disk, this success suggests that the IMF-averaged nucleosynthetic yields of α - and Fe-peak elements are largely universal. This predictability makes the empirical yields immediately useful: embedding them in stellar population synthesis models will improve inferences on stellar populations and star formation histories, while incorporating them into cosmological simulations will produce more observationally motivated predictions.

picks.title: From “KGeP” to the Protonated P4-like Anion (HGe3P)2– and the Endohedral Zintl Cluster [Mn@Ge10P2]3–
picks.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
picks.abstract: P4-like Zintl anions (Tt2Pn2)2–, which combine the properties of the formally underlying homoatomic units, Tt44– or Pn4 (Tt = tetrel, group 14 element; Pn = pnictogen, group 15 element), are versatile starting materials for ternary clusters. However, not all of the theoretically possible Tt/Pn elemental combinations are accessible, and not all of them show decent reactivity. A particularly challenging elemental combination is that of Ge and P, in contrast to homoatomic P4 or Gen4– (n = 4, 9) that are widely used for corresponding reactions. The only report on a trinuclear complex, [Cd3(Ge3P)3]3–, obtained by reacting a “(Ge2P2)2–” anion, raised questions about the assumed 2:2 ratio of the atoms in the starting material. Herein, we aimed at clarifying the mystery about the composition and identifying a means of accessing new M/Ge/P-based cluster architectures. Regarding the first, we disclosed that the anion is actually not a 2:2 unit, but the first protonated version of a binary P4-like Zintl anion, (HGe3P)2–, which finally rationalizes the composition of the previously reported trinuclear complex. The anion was obtained as its [K(crypt-222)]+ salt by the extraction of “KGeP” with ethane-1,2-diamine (en), acting as a Brønsted acid toward the Zintl anion. 1H NMR spectroscopy and computations of NMR chemical shifts confirmed the presence of the protonated anion in the salt and in solution. As (HGe3P)2– did not show the desired reactivity, we used the more reductive extraction solution of “KGeP” in situ for a follow-up reaction with [Mn(Cp*)2], yielding the first Ge/P-based endohedral Zintl cluster, [Mn@Ge10P2]3–.

picks.title: Flat-band-induced integer doping and phase transition in monolayer graphene
picks.abstract: van der Waals heterostructures are stabilized by a delicate balance between van der Waals, elastic and Coulomb energies 1–4 . Because the interfaces are not covalently bonded, the constituent crystals can slide, rotate and reconstruct, resulting in several possible competing structural phases 2,5,6 . However, controlled tuning of this balance, and hence dynamical control over the stacking, has yet to be achieved. Here we report a dynamical heterostructure in which monolayer graphene is doubly aligned to bulk hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) and monolayer hexagonal boron nitride (mhBN) on either side. In such a system, a global structural phase transition, manifested as a change of crystalline symmetry observed by scanning tunnelling microscopy, could be induced by gating, magnetic field or temperature. This structural transition is accompanied by an exotic electronic transition: the doping of graphene switches between discrete levels, corresponding to an exact integer number of electrons or holes per moiré plaquette. We attribute this integer doping to charge trapping in localized, strain-induced pseudo-Landau levels (flat bands in reciprocal space 7–12 ), produced by moiré reconstruction (strongly enhanced by the mhBN). Electrical control of coupled structural and electronic phase transitions provides a route to engineering strain-induced flat bands and strain–Coulomb correlations in van der Waals heterostructures.

picks.title: Hadean mantle depletion and 3.95-Gyr subduction implied by North China rocks
picks.abstract: The scarcity of terrestrial rocks older than 3.9 billion years (Ga) has hindered our understanding of Earth’s early evolution, fueling persistent debates on how and when the first continental crust formed and plate tectonics started. Currently, the only unequivocally documented >3.9 Ga rocks are from the Acasta Gneiss Complex, Canada 1–3. Here we report a newly discovered 3.95 Ga trondhjemitic gneiss from eastern Hebei, North China Craton, where 3.95 Ga magmatic zircon records elevated δ18O values (average +6.77 ± 0.23‰) and positive εHf(t) (weighted mean +1.45 ± 0.27), indicating a low-temperature altered basaltic source that originated from a Hadean depleted mantle. In contrast to the low-pressure origin inferred for the ca. 4.0 Ga Acasta rocks 2, the 3.95 Ga trondhjemitic gneiss reported here exhibits geochemical signatures attributed to a high-pressure origin 4. Thermodynamic and trace element modelling demonstrates that its parental magma formed via low degree (8–16%) melting of basaltic crust at >1.6 GPa and 740–820 ℃, suggesting rapid burial of (near-)surface‑altered oceanic crust to mantle depths along a cool thermal gradient. We propose that this rapid burial was most likely achieved through a transient subduction event.

picks.title: Hydroxamate Reticular Chemistry beyond Metals: Single-Crystalline Two- and Three-Dimensional Boron–Hydroxamate Covalent Organic Frameworks
picks.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
picks.abstract: Hydroxamate chelation has already enabled robust metal–organic frameworks. Here, to move the corresponding reticular chemistry beyond metal nodes, hydroxamate chelation has been integrated within heteroleptic tetracoordinate B(O,O)(N)(C) centers to construct four single-crystalline boron–hydroxamate covalent organic frameworks, namely SUM-306–SUM-309. Bayesian optimization enabled the growth of diffraction-quality SUM-306 single crystals, while linker isomerism and functionalization yielded a series spanning two-dimensional hcb and three-dimensional pcu-h frameworks. Structural comparison reveals extended anti-B–phenylene–B arrangements in SUM-306 and SUM-307 and folded syn arrangements in SUM-308 and SUM-309, associated with their respective two- and three-dimensional propagation. Solid-state NMR spectroscopy, B K-edge XANES, and electronic-structure calculations support tetracoordinate boron formation and differentiated yet substantial bonding throughout the B(O,O)(N)(C) environment. As a representative of the series, SUM-308 retains accessible microporosity, exhibits a BET surface area of 1279.9 m2 g–1, and preferentially adsorbs and dynamically separates CO2 from N2. These results extend hydroxamate reticular chemistry beyond metals and establish a mixed-linkage strategy combining chelation, donor–acceptor coordination, and covalent anchoring for single-crystalline boron-based framework construction.

picks.title: Could All Rules Have Goals?
picks.abstract: I argue that not all belief-relative normative principles can be represented as requiring the maximization of expected utility. The argument imposes no limits on the distinctions that utility functions can draw, but relies instead on a connection between decision-theoretic representability and uncertainty about one’s own beliefs. By contrast, I argue that evidence-relative normative principles, which say what to do given what would be rational to believe, always admit of such a representation, so long as uncertainty about epistemic rationality is limited in independently plausible ways.

more.title: Odd-Parity Magnons in the Haldane-Hubbard Model from Topological Exciton Condensation
more.abstract: Collective excitations in condensed matter can carry nontrivial topology and provide information about quantum phases beyond their ground-state properties. At the same time, the recent emergence of altermagnetism and related nonrelativistic spin-split electronic states raises the question of how unconventional magnetic symmetry is encoded in their collective excitations. Here, we uncover a continuous evolution from topological excitons to odd-parity magnons across an interaction-driven magnetic transition in the paradigmatic Haldane-Hubbard model. In the paramagnetic phase, our newly found sharp topological excitons soften and condense into a collinear Néel state, where they evolve into Goldstone magnons displaying characteristic f -wave spin splitting. The topology of these collective modes is tied to the underlying electronic topology, such that an electron bandgap closing enforces a magnon bandgap closing, changing the magnon topology. Our results establish a direct connection between topological collective excitations and nonrelativistic odd-parity spin splittings, with potential realizations in Floquet-driven materials and cold atomic gases.

more.title: Magic without entanglement: Exact revivals and their Fisher information origin
more.abstract: Magic and entanglement are independent quantum resources, yet their exact relation in many-body dynamics has remained elusive. We uncover two structural principles. First, at any stabilizer state, the curvature of the second stabilizer R'enyi entropy under an arbitrary Hermitian generator equals the quantum Fisher information up to a fixed normalization, creating a bidirectional bridge between computational and metrological resources. Second, for commuting Ising evolution on any forest graph, a Clifford pruning circuit yields the full stabilizer-R'enyi family at arbitrary size and in any spatial embedding, thereby furnishing a graph-theoretic construction of families with finite magic density and vanishing entanglement density in the thermodynamic limit. We solve two paradigmatic one-dimensional realizations central to quantum simulation—an Ising quench and a kicked Floquet chain—exactly for arbitrary system size and directly in the thermodynamic limit, revealing finite magic density with vanishing entanglement density, distinct magic and entanglement revival periods, and Clifford points with zero magic but finite bipartite entanglement. The same tangent geometry fixes initial growth and perturbative revival lifting, and a replica cluster expansion establishes the stability of thermodynamic magic minima uniformly in system size. Large scale Pauli-basis matrix-product-state calculations verify all predictions, and the tangent bridge yields a concrete protocol for detecting magic near stabilizer reference states through established quantum-Fisher-information measurements.

more.title: Electronic correlations and dynamical screening with ab initio quantum embedding
more.abstract: First-principles descriptions of correlated quantum materials require a simultaneous treatment of strong local many-body effects and nonlocal dynamical screening. We present an efficient fully self-consistent implementation of G W +EDMFT that combines nonlocal correlations at the G W level with a non-perturbative treatment of local correlations within extended dynamical mean-field theory (EDMFT), with a well-defined double-counting correction and a self-consistently determined impurity interaction. Self-consistency in both the Green’s function and the dynamically screened interaction is essential for describing screening processes across energy scales. A key ingredient that makes it computationally feasible is the compression of two-particle correlation functions using interpolative separable density fitting (ISDF). Applying the scheme to the Mott insulator SrMnO 3 and the correlated metal LaNiO 3 , we show that the self-consistent effective local interaction resolves the overscreening inherent to constrained-RPA approaches. For SrMnO 3 , this stabilizes a Mott-insulating state in quantitative agreement with experiment, while for LaNiO 3 local EDMFT corrections yield a quasiparticle mass enhancement consistent with ARPES. These results establish fully self-consistent G W +EDMFT as a reliable framework for strongly correlated quantum materials.

more.title: Relationship between antibunching and entanglement in resonance fluorescence
more.abstract: Photon antibunching in resonance fluorescence - the emission from a single, resonantly driven two-level quantum emitter - is a paradigmatic signature of nonclassical light. Photon entanglement, by contrast, manifests as correlations that can defy any classical description and is typically regarded as a distinct quantum effect. Here, we experimentally extract pairs of narrowband, time-bin–entangled photons from the antibunched resonance fluorescence of a single trapped atom. We verify entanglement by using the CHSH Bell inequality as an entanglement witness and by reconstructing the two-photon density matrix. The observed correlations vanish when the coincidence time window exceeds the antibunching timescale, revealing underlying multimode entanglement in the emitted field. Our results establish a direct link between photon antibunching and photon–photon entanglement, connecting two canonical signatures of nonclassical light.

more.title: First Principles Magnetohydrodynamical Theory for the Expanding Box Model: Effects on Expansion-induced Alfvén Wave Reflection
more.abstract: The expanding box model (EBM) has been widely employed to simulate multiscale plasma phenomena in the expanding solar wind by transforming the MHD equations to a comoving, noninertial frame. However, traditional formulations have suffered from historical ambiguity regarding the physical separation between the comoving and inertial reference frames, primarily arising from a classical approximation of an invariant magnetic field between them. To resolve this inconsistency, we reformulate the EBM from first principles using a fully covariant approach. Here, we model the expanding solar wind frame as an anisotropic expanding spacetime metric, allowing us to incorporate radial acceleration profiles and differential transverse expansion, ensuring that all physical fields are correctly transformed by expansion. We demonstrate that asymmetries identified in previous EBM-MHD literature are direct consequences of neglecting the tensorial scaling of the magnetic field. Our covariant treatment eliminates these residues, restoring symmetry in the comoving frame. Projecting our system back into the inertial frame clarifies the distinction between local plasma dynamics and plasma expansion, revealing the anisotropy of the Parker spiral as a geometric projection. Furthermore, linear wave analysis using Elsässer variables reveals that plasma expansion induces a low-frequency cutoff and geometric damping. Numerical integration demonstrates that expansion drives the reflection of Alfvén waves, generating counter-propagating modes primarily at low frequencies relative to the expansion rate, while high frequencies converge to the WKB approximation. This provides a consistent foundation for simulations, establishing that expansion can serve as a source of counter-propagating waves…

more.title: The Study of Detailed Morphology of Milky Way Dwarf Galaxies: Draco and Boötes I
more.abstract: We present a photometric study of the outer stellar structures of the Milky Way (MW) dwarf spheroidal galaxies (dSphs) Draco and Boötes I, using deep wide-field imaging data. The old main-sequence stars are used to trace their spatial distributions beyond their tidal radii. We derive global structural parameters and radial profiles of number density, ellipticity, and position angle from their stellar distributions. Draco and Boötes I show contrasting features. Draco shows no prominent extended stellar distribution, although weak elongations are detected toward the eastern and northwestern directions. Its stellar distribution remains relatively compact compared with its estimated Jacobi tidal radius ( r J = 57 ′ . 2 − 11.1 + 13.5 ), suggesting that the stellar component is tightly bound by its gravitational potential. In contrast, the radial number-density profiles of Boötes I along several directions show excess from the best-fit exponential profile outside of around r ∼ 2 0 ′ , near the estimated Jacobi radius ( r J = 21 ′ . 6 − 7.6 + 9.3 ). In addition, the ellipticity of Draco decreases with radius, whereas that of Boötes I increases toward larger radii. Boötes I also exhibits a prominent S-shaped stellar structure extending approximately along its orbital direction. Together, the radial density excess, increasing ellipticity, and S-shaped morphology suggest that the outer stellar structure of Boötes I may trace tidal tails produced by interactions with the MW. The contrasting morphologies of Draco and Boötes I further suggest that the response of dwarf galaxies to the MW tidal field may depend not only on their orbital histories, but also on the internal structure of their dark matter halos.

more.title: CLAS+: A Large Catalog of Changing-look Active Galactic Nucleus Candidates Selected through S-PLUS Narrowband Photometry
more.abstract: Changing-look active galactic nuclei (CLAGN) exhibit rapid spectral transitions on timescales of months to years, challenging standard AGN unification models and providing unique insight into accretion-disk variability and obscuration processes. Despite their scientific importance, systematic searches for CLAGN remain limited by the scarcity of multiepoch spectroscopy and the difficulty of constructing large samples efficiently. We introduce CLAS+, a catalog constructed by comparing synthetic photometry derived from DESI DR1 and Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) DR17 spectra with contemporaneous narrowband imaging from the S-PLUS survey. Applying our pipeline to a parent sample of 98,139 quasars, we select high-confidence CLAGN candidates above a threshold of reduced chi-squared χ r 2 > 15 . We identify 3554 strong CLAGN candidates, corresponding to 3.6% of the parent sample. This selected fraction is conditional on the adopted criterion and should not be interpreted as an intrinsic CLAGN occurrence rate. Cross-matching with existing CLAGN compilations shows that CLAS+ identifies a large population of previously unreported high-priority candidates (3481). Among the spectroscopic–photometric comparisons with reliable temporal classification, 40% are classified as photometric turn-on, 41% as intermediate, and 19% as turn-off. We also find an apparent redshift dependence in the relative fractions, with photometric turn-on candidates becoming more common at higher redshifts within the CLAS+ selected sample. Therefore, narrowband photometry provides a powerful and efficient alternative to purely spectroscopic searches for identifying CLAGN candidates at scale. CLAS+ substantially expands the known CLAGN candidate population and provides a valuable target list for future…

more.title: Constraints on the Schwarzschild Black Hole in a Generalized Dehnen-type (1, 4, γ ) Dark Matter Halo via the S2 Star Orbit around Sgr A*
more.abstract: The distribution of dark matter (DM) halo around supermassive black holes (BHs) may leave observable imprints on stellar dynamics near galactic centers. Motivated by this, we investigate the orbital motion of the S2 star in the spacetime of a recently derived generalized Schwarzschild BH solution embedded in a Dehnen-type (1, 4, γ ) DM halo, considering it as a possible model for Sgr A ⋆ at the center of the Milky Way. Unlike previous studies restricted to specific values of the halo parameter γ , the present solution describes the fully generalized case with arbitrary γ . We derive the corresponding equations of motion and obtain the associated pericenter shift over one orbital period. Using observational data of the S2 star, we constrain the parameters of the Schwarzschild–Dehnen BH–DM system through a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analysis. Our MCMC analysis provides constraints on the parameter γ of the generalized Dehnen-type DM halo. The posterior medians of γ with 68% credible intervals are γ = 0.65 2 − 0.446 + 0.435 and γ = 0.77 1 − 0.522 + 0.486 for Dataset 1 from T. Do et al. and Dataset 2 from S. Gillessen et al., respectively. The corresponding one-sided 95% upper credible limits are γ < 1.238 and γ < 1.389. If the halo is instead normalized to the observed local DM density at solar distance, ρ DM (8 kpc) ≃ 0.01 M ⊙ pc −3 , the 95% upper limits become γ < 1.949 and γ < 1.931 for Dataset 1 and Dataset 2, respectively. The analysis shows that the S2 orbital motion provides constraints on the parameter γ of the DM halo profile, while the characteristic halo density ρ s and scale radius r s exhibit a strong degeneracy and remain sensitive to the adopted prior ranges.

more.title: Tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity
more.abstract: Tropical land-use intensification threatens global biodiversity, yet most assessments of tropical agricultural landscapes focus on local-scale biodiversity, overlooking how land use restructures biodiversity across space and multiple taxa. Here we provide an ecosystem-wide assessment of 24 taxonomic groups across all domains of life—encompassing 40,049 species—along a land-use intensification gradient from lowland forests to intensively managed smallholder cash-crop monocultures in Indonesian landscapes. Despite widespread losses of landscape and local multidiversity 1 in monocultures (approximately 78% and 50%, respectively), we found no evidence for consistent community homogenization with land-use intensification. Instead, monocultures exhibit a systematic shift from turnover to nestedness for aboveground taxa. Such patterns of differentiation may mask trajectories towards biotic homogenization via early stages of assemblage simplification. Biotic differentiation has the potential to partly mitigate biodiversity losses by positively affecting γ-diversity. This opens management options, including the conservation of existing remnants of traditional agriculture and the implementation of sustainable management practices 2–4 . Our results demonstrate that tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity not only through species loss, but also via a pervasive reorganization of community composition across trophic levels. Conserving tropical biodiversity, therefore, requires a multi-taxon, landscape-scale perspective that explicitly integrates agricultural land uses with the protection of natural and semi-natural habitats to reconcile agricultural production and conservation.

more.title: Ferroptosis in cancer cells triggers PGE2 production for tumour immune escape
more.abstract: Ferroptosis, a form of cell death induced by overwhelming membrane lipid peroxidation, is a vulnerability of many cancers, including cancers resistant to current molecular and immune-based therapies 1–7 . Triggering of ferroptosis therefore provides an opportunity to achieve elimination of difficult-to-treat cancers 1–4,8,9 . Studies in mouse cancer models have demonstrated that anticancer immunity, mediated by dendritic cells (DCs) and CD8 + T cells, is essential for effective tumour eradication by ferroptosis-inducing strategies 10–13 . However, ferroptotic cells limit this response 8–10,14 , resulting in immune escape and tumour growth through mechanisms that remain unclear. Here we demonstrate that ferroptotic cancer cells activate a molecular program resulting in aberrant production of prostaglandin E 2 (PGE 2 ), which limits the stimulation of anticancer CD8 + T cell responses by type 1 conventional DCs (cDC1s), thereby promoting immune escape. In ferroptotic cancer cells, lipid peroxidation-mediated membrane permeabilization enables Ca 2+ influx, which activates p38 MAPK signalling and thereby drives PGE 2 production. This signalling axis is uncoupled from cancer cell death and can be targeted to selectively interfere with immune-inhibitory PGE 2 production while preserving ferroptotic cancer cell elimination. In the context of cancer cell ferroptosis, ablation of PGE 2 production or disrupting PGE 2 signalling restores cDC1-mediated anticancer CD8 + T cell responses and leads to effective tumour elimination. Our findings identify a key mechanism that limits antitumour immunity and prevents tumour elimination upon ferroptosis induction in cancer cells, which could be exploited for cancer therapy.

more.title: UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss
more.abstract: TDP-43 nuclear depletion is a defining pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia that induces widespread cryptic splicing defects in hundreds of transcripts 1–8 . Despite this, whether TDP-43 loss affects synaptic function has remained unclear. Here we show that TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact but suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication. Genetic correction of a single cryptic splicing event in UNC13A was sufficient to rescue these deficits. We developed splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides that correct UNC13A cryptic splicing in human cortical and spinal motor neurons and in a humanized mouse model. In human neurons this intervention restored spontaneous and evoked synaptic vesicle release, release probability at individual synapses and wider network synchrony. Together, this establishes UNC13A splice correction as a mechanistically defined and genetically validated therapeutic strategy relevant to roughly 97% of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and roughly 50% of patients with frontotemporal dementia with TDP-43 pathology.

more.title: Mechanisms of Ammonia Synthesis over Ru Low- and High-Index Surfaces Based on Density Functional Theory Calculations
more.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
more.abstract: Ammonia is a vital compound for the future, with significant potential in energy applications, such as hydrogen-powered vehicles, and in agriculture as a key ingredient in fertilizers essential for food production. Traditionally, ammonia has been synthesized via the Haber-Bosch process using an iron catalyst, which requires high temperatures (400 to 500 °C) and pressures (about 200 atm), leading to a substantial carbon footprint and energy costs. Ruthenium is a promising alternative catalyst due to its higher intrinsic catalytic activity, allowing for ammonia synthesis under milder conditions. This paper presents a detailed Density Functional Theory (DFT) study of the elementary steps involved in ammonia production across five distinct facets: Ru(0001), Ru(10–10), Ru(11–20), Ru(11–21), and Ru(10–11). Using vibrational frequency analysis, we applied zero-point energy (ZPE), enthalpic, and entropic corrections at 80 °C. We also examined the competition with the hydrogen evolution reaction. Ultimately, we find that the step-edge coordination of the Ru(11–21) surface offers the most favorable thermodynamic pathway for NH3 formation and the most efficient catalytic performance. Nudged elastic band calculations on Ru(11–21) show that hydrogenation mediated by coadsorbed water has low barriers and that NH3 desorption is the most demanding step. Further, the Ru(11–21) surface favors water dissociation, while H2 evolution on the clean surface is uphill by 0.5 eV in free energy.

more.title: De Novo Design of Single–Crystalline Peptide Frameworks Enables Structure–Encoded Molecular Recognition
more.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
more.abstract: Molecular recognition by proteins underlies many biological processes and depends on the precise spatial organization of functional residues within well-defined binding pockets. Synthetic peptide assembly, however, is frequently biased toward anisotropic fibrillar or other low-dimensional morphologies, owing in part to the directional nature of peptide hydrogen-bonding networks, which can hinder the formation of ordered, structurally encoded binding cavities with biomimetic recognition properties. Here we show that coordination-driven β-sheet reprogramming overcomes this constraint by redirecting peptide assembly into single-crystalline peptide frameworks. Through de novo peptide design, we incorporate tyrosine, a residue that often plays a key role in protein molecular recognition, as a functional side chain, while metal–peptide connectivity suppresses fibrillar growth and decouples backbone packing from side-chain organization, thereby orienting tyrosine residues along internal channel surfaces to generate chiral recognition environments. The resulting frameworks exhibit high chemical and mechanical robustness, allow the spatial organization of tyrosine residues to be resolved crystallographically, and display excellent stereoselective recognition performance toward structurally complex glucocorticoids and chiral pharmaceuticals. Molecular dynamics simulations suggest that tyrosine residues dynamically interact with guest molecules during recognition. Our findings provide a design principle for constructing crystalline peptide frameworks with biomimetic molecular recognition, expanding the structural and functional scope of synthetic peptide materials.

more.title: A Three-Motif-Based One-Dimensional Covalent Organic Framework as an Efficient Cathode Material for Stable Rechargeable Sodium-Ion Batteries
more.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
more.abstract: Crystalline one-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (1D COFs) hold great promise for diverse applications; however, their synthesis remains challenging, as it requires simultaneous control over chain dimensionality and crystallization of polymeric chains that are intrinsically prone to entanglement. Here, we show that benzo[1,2-b:4,5-b′]difuran-2,6(3H,7H)-dione (BDFO), in the presence of isoquinoline, effectively compels the trifunctional monomer 2,4,6-tris(4-formylphenyl)-1,3,5-triazine (TPFT) to polymerize as a V-shaped ditopic linker, affording 1D zigzag chains that stack in a staggered arrangement to form the crystalline porous framework (CityU-31). CityU-31 exhibits a rectangular nanowire morphology with well-defined lattice fringes, a narrow pore-size distribution of 1–2 nm, and a surface area of 185 m2 g–1. Importantly, the V-shaped connectivity leaves one formyl group at each TPFT unit unreacted, and these pendant aldehydes serve as built-in handles for postsynthetic functionalization. As a proof of concept, a third motif was covalently linked via Knoevenagel condensation, converting the aldehyde groups into cyano functionalities to yield CityU-31-CN. Endowed with the cyano-decorated 1D backbone, CityU-31-CN delivers an extended voltage window (0.8–3.5 V), a high capacity of 160 mAh g–1 at 0.1 A g–1, and outstanding cycling stability (>10,000 cycles). The intrinsic backbone reactivity of CityU-31 thus offers a versatile platform for postsynthetic modification, greatly expanding the application scope of crystalline 1D polymers.

more.title: Planar-Chiral Metal Clusters Direct Polarization-Responsive Supercrystals
more.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
more.abstract: Chiral metal clusters are promising atomically precise building blocks for hierarchical chiral materials, but their programmed assembly into structurally resolved supercrystals with traceable chirality transfer remains challenging. Here, we show that planar-chiral Cu5 clusters can serve as symmetry-defined modules for constructing polarization-responsive supercrystals. Through single-site capping control and symmetry-matched linker-directed coordination assembly, the Cu5 unit is organized into monomeric, dimeric, trimeric, and helical crystalline architectures, thereby enabling chirality to be traced from discrete clusters to higher-order supercrystalline structures. Single-crystal analyses reveal how the planar chirality of the cluster is encoded locally and propagated through distinct, orientationally ordered packing sequences. Quantitative Mueller matrix measurements show architecture-dependent circular and linear optical responses, including circular and linear retardance, which correlate with the crystallographic orientation and packing sequence of the Cu5 units, particularly Cu···Cu bonding. This work establishes planar-chiral metal clusters as versatile, stereochemically programmable synthons, providing a quantitative framework that links cluster-level chirality, arrangement orientation, and macroscopic polarization-dependent optical responses. The strategy offers a novel modular route to structurally defined chiral supercrystals, in which optical polarization responses can be traced to atomically resolved anisotropic sequences of chiral cluster assembly.

more.title: TransA-MERFISH reveals divergent post-retinal direction-selective circuits
more.abstract: A major goal in neuroscience is to map the transformation of information as it flows through the brain. For example, neurons at many levels of the visual hierarchy are attuned to motion direction1–5. However, links between motion-selective computations and cell types at various stages of the visual hierarchy remain unidentified. A key first step in delineating these relationships is to map the wiring diagrams that connect different motion-selective cell types. Here we establish a systematic, cell-type-specific circuit-mapping method, combining an anterograde trans-neuronal fluorescent tracer (mWGA–mCherry)6 with spatial transcriptomics (multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH))7,8 to establish TransA-MERFISH. We used TransA-MERFISH to comprehensively map the synaptic target cell types of four retinal ganglion cell subclasses in superior colliculus (SC) at cell-type resolution. These experiments unexpectedly revealed that retinal on–off direction-selective ganglion cells (ooDSGCs) innervate several direction-selective SC cell types, but do not innervate a SC cell type that was previously reported to display strong direction-selective responses. We validated these results using orthogonal approaches and demonstrated the sensitivity and specificity of TransA-MERFISH. Functional studies of SC activity before and after ablation of retinal direction-selective circuits confirmed that these computationally distinct, ooDSGC-dependent and -independent direction-selective cell types are commingled in SC. Together, our study establishes TransA-MERFISH as a robust framework for mapping wiring diagrams at the cell-type level and uncovers divergent computational mechanisms of motion detection in early visual processing. more.title: The microbial world of male reproduction
more.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
more.abstract: The last decade has brought renewed interest to microbial influences on host biology, yet the roles of microbes in host reproductive biology are underappreciated and often defined by a profound maternal bias. This perspective synthesizes emerging evidence across the tree of life to highlight the paternal microbiome as an overlooked driver of fitness, reproductive output, and intergenerational health, impacting epigenetic sculpting of the sperm and embryo, sexual transmission of microbes, and male gamete functions. These contributions indicate that mating can involve interactions between holobionts rather than simply the union of the maternal and paternal genomes. Thus, uniting male reproduction with the growing generalizations of microbial symbiosis guides several conceptual, theoretical, and empirical avenues for research in the life sciences.

more.title: Carbon dioxide and amorphous water ices in the debris disk around β Pictoris
more.abstract: The star β Pictoris is orbited by a dusty debris disk, within which planet formation is occurring. The outer disk is sufficiently far from the star that volatile molecules are expected to freeze into solid ices. We observed the β Pictoris disk in the near-infrared using the James Webb Space Telescope. The spectrum shows features due to amorphous water ice (<7% crystallinity) and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) ice in both the 12 CO 2 and 13 CO 2 isotopologues. We infer that the CO 2 ice is intimately mixed with the water ice at a ratio of 1:10. This implies that the ices formed in cold conditions, likely in the interstellar medium. Frequent collisions within the debris disk are required to explain the observed uniform distribution of icy dust grains.

more.title: Novel gene therapy lets drug dampen brain cell activity, reducing seizures

more.title: Manufacturing Halide Perovskite PV: Considerations To Enable Wide-Scale Deployment
more.abstract: Perovskite photovoltaic (PV) technologies have witnessed rapid progress during the past decade and are rapidly approaching the stage of commercialization. With small-area perovskite solar cells rapidly overtaking many conventional PV technology records, scaling and material stability have become roadblocks to commercialization. Wide-scale market adoption of perovskite-based PV technologies can only be achieved when key challenges for all three pillars of efficiency, scalability, and stability/reliability are successfully addressed. Although lab-scale material stability and performance are often measured in controlled laboratory settings, module-scale reliability must be demonstrated in real-world conditions. Here, we aim to provide a comprehensive review of the current challenges to commercialization as well as recent innovations and pathways to overcome these challenges. For recent material and processing innovations, we focus on solution-based approaches, but we also briefly discuss some vapor-based approaches. For reliability considerations, we review module packaging approaches, current state of real-world demonstrations, and efforts to field test modules. We also discuss economic considerations and potential next steps on remaining challenges toward commercialization of perovskite PV technologies.

more.title: Contemporary synthetic tools for the total synthesis of natural products
more.abstract: The field of total synthesis is often viewed as a testing ground for newly developed synthetic methodologies. This Tutorial Review highlights the application of contemporary synthetic tools in the total synthesis of natural products over the past five years, including photocatalysis, electrochemistry, biocatalysis, skeletal editing, flow chemistry and mechanochemistry. Significant developments in each respective field that have advanced the state-of-the-art are a particular focus, showcasing the cutting-edge methods used in modern synthetic organic chemistry, and demonstrating their potential for application in complex settings.

more.title: Luminescent radicals – synthesis, photophysics and applications
more.abstract: Although known for over a century, radicals have only now begun playing a role in the chemistry of π-conjugated materials. Over the past two decades, following Juliá's discovery that a Ballester-type radical bearing a single carbazole substituent can achieve a photoluminescence quantum yield of 53%, luminescent radicals have progressed from a scientific curiosity to a well-established research field. Although the chemical space of luminescent radicals is rather limited and the details of their photophysics still require better understanding, the field continues to fascinate and challenge researchers. In this review, we present all aspects of the chemistry of luminescent radicals, starting with general photophysical considerations, moving through synthetic developments and structure-property relationship, before discussing computational aspects and various applications. A detailed analysis of the advances made since 2006 highlights the contributions of multiple research groups that have continually expanded the structural landscape of luminescent radicals. Particular emphasis is placed on synthetic aspects, as the availability of robust synthetic methodologies is often a bottleneck, limiting progress in materials-oriented research.

more.title: Incorporating Noncanonical Amino Acids for Protein Structure Analysis: Site-Directed Spin Labeling CW and Pulsed EPR Approaches
more.abstract: Site-directed spin labeling in combination with electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy (SDSL–EPR) has emerged as a powerful and highly adaptable platform probing protein structure and dynamics with residue-level precision. In its classical strategy, a stable paramagnetic label, most commonly a nitroxide radical, but not only, is covalently introduced at a predefined position, typically through an engineered cysteine residue. Continuous-wave (cw) EPR spectroscopy provides sensitivity to protein dynamics across a broad range of time scales (and techniques), from backbone motions (ps-ns) to protein complex assembly and conformational transitions (ms-s) or characterization of protein conformational exchange (μs-ms). Pulsed EPR methodologies, particularly double electron–electron resonance (DEER), provide access to long-range distance distributions in the nanometer regime (ca. 2–8 nm) through the measurement of dipolar interactions between pairs of spin labels. Recent developments in the genetic encoding of noncanonical amino acids (ncAAs) have substantially expanded the scope of SDSL–EPR by overcoming the intrinsic limitations associated with cysteine-based labeling. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of ncAA-based spin-labeling strategies for SDSL–EPR, discuss the repertoire of reported spin labels and their synthetic routes, and highlight representative applications in structural investigations of proteins in vitro as well as in cellular environments.

more.title: “Sit Nice!”: Peer Culture, Teacher Capacity, and Joint Socialization Efforts in Preschool
more.abstract: Preschools instill soft skills that are crucial to children’s life outcomes. As preschool access expands, research and policy often focus on improving teacher quality. This focus downplays how much teachers’ efforts may depend on children’s peers. Drawing on two years of ethnography, I highlight two important aspects of socialization: teachers’ capacity to deliver messages in the moment, and peers’ tendency to support those messages. I compare socialization processes at two race- and class-segregated preschools. Three interrelated classroom conditions—children’s enrollment, attendance, and challenging behaviors—mattered for socialization interactions. Teachers at both preschools pursued socialization goals of instilling safe and formal classroom behaviors. At the affluent, majority-White preschool, teachers had a greater capacity to coach children in the moment, and peers had a culture of supporting teacher messages. At the low-income, racially diverse preschool, children placed the authority to coach classroom behavior in their teachers, who were pressed for time. I argue that socialization agents jointly influence behavior. In segregated preschools, teachers may shape classroom behavior to unequal extents, preventing early learning settings from disrupting future inequalities.

more.title: Temporal Complexity Hierarchies in Solvable Quantum Many-Body Dynamics
more.abstract: The influence matrix (IM) provides a powerful framework for characterizing nonequilibrium quantum many-body dynamics by encoding multitime correlations into tensor-network states. Understanding how its computational complexity relates to underlying dynamics is crucial for both theoretical insight and practical utility yet remains largely unexplored despite a few case studies. Here, we address this question for a family of brickwork quantum circuits ranging from integrable to chaotic regimes. Using tools from geometric group theory, we identify three qualitatively distinct scalings of temporal entanglement entropy, establishing a hierarchy of computational resources required for accurate tensor-network representations of the IM for these models. We further analyze the memory structure of the IM and distinguish between classical and quantum temporal correlations. In particular, for certain examples, we identify effectively classical IMs that admit an efficient Monte Carlo algorithm for computing multitime correlations. In more generic settings without an explicit classical description of the IM, we introduce an operational measure of quantum memory with an experimental protocol and discuss examples exhibiting long-time genuinely quantum correlations. Our results establish a new connection between quantum many-body dynamics and group theory, providing fresh insights into the complexity of the IM and its intricate connection to the physical characteristics of the dynamics.

more.title: Spectral Small-Incremental Entangling: Breaking Quasipolynomial Complexity Barriers in Long-Range Interacting Systems
more.abstract: How the detailed entanglement structure emerges from quantum dynamics remains a fundamental challenge motivated by recent advances in quantum simulators and information processing. As a central milestone, the small-incremental-entangling (SIE) theorem bounds the entanglement-entropy growth rate but does not control the entanglement spectrum itself. In this work, we define the spectral-entangling strength, which quantifies how strongly an operator can reshape the distribution of Schmidt coefficients across a bipartition. We then prove a spectral-SIE theorem: for Rényi index α ≥ 1 / 2 , the growth rate of Rényi-entanglement entropies admits a universal bound. Remarkably, our bound at α = 1 / 2 is both qualitatively and quantitatively optimal; below this threshold ( α < 1 / 2 ), no universal speed limit on entanglement growth can exist. This result yields a sharp 1 / s 2 threshold in the tail of the ordered squared Schmidt coefficients, or equivalently in the entanglement-spectrum weights (with s the Schmidt index). It enables rigorous truncation-based-error control and establishes a quantitative link between entanglement-spectrum structure and computational complexity. As a practical highlight, for one-dimensional power-law interactions 1 / r η with η > 2 , this implies matrix-product-state approximations with bond dimension polynomial in ( n / ε ) for ground states, real-time evolved states, and Gibbs states, thereby closing the quasipolynomial gap, where n is the system size, and ε denotes the target approximation error in the relevant state or operator norm. By controlling Rényi entanglement, we further obtain a rigorous truncation-error bound for the time-dependent density-matrix renormalization-group scheme analyzed here. more.title: Tomographic Electron Flow in Confined Geometries: Beyond the Dual-Relaxation-Time Approximation
more.abstract: Hydrodynamiclike electron flows are typically modeled using the Stokes-Ohm equation or a kinetic description that is based on a dual-relaxation-time approximation. Such models assume a short intrinsic mean free path ℓ e due to momentum-conserving electronic scattering and a large extrinsic mean free path ℓ MR due to momentum-relaxing impurity scattering. This assumption, however, is overly simplistic and falls short at low temperatures, where it is known from exact diagonalization studies of the electronic collision integrals that another large electronic mean free path ℓ o emerges that describes long-lived odd electron modes—this is sometimes known as the tomographic effect. Here, using a matched asymptotic expansion of the underlying Fermi-liquid kinetic equation with multiple electron relaxation times, we derive a transport theory for tomographic flows in arbitrary smooth boundary geometries. Our key results are a set of governing equations for the electron density and electron current, their slip boundary conditions (which are applied at diffuse boundaries), and boundary layer corrections near diffuse edges. We find that the tomographic effect strongly modifies previous hydrodynamic theories for electron flows: In particular, (i) a local equilibrium is established in the bulk, where the flow is governed by Stokes-Ohm-like equations with significant finite-wavelength corrections, (ii) the velocity slip condition at the boundary is strongly modified and not accounted for by the widely used hydrodynamic slip-length condition, (iii) a large kinetic boundary layer of width ∼ ℓ e ℓ o arises near diffuse boundaries, which is much larger than in conventional near-hydrodynamic theories, and (iv) all these effects are strongly suppressed by an external magnetic field. more.title: Analyzing post-transcriptional regulation in stochastic gene expression models using partitioned Poisson arrivals
more.abstract: Gene expression is a stochastic process that allows for fluctuations in protein levels that can give rise to phenotypic heterogeneity within a population of genetically identical cells. Thus, there is great interest in quantifying how natural variation (noise) in gene expression is impacted by cellular control mechanisms, such as the various mechanisms pertaining to post-transcriptional regulation. Although previous research has developed a general analytical framework to compute the exact moments of mRNA distributions for any promoter-based regulatory motif, and the exact mRNA distribution itself in some cases, a similar framework for protein fluctuations is currently lacking. Here, we invoke the partitioning property of Poisson arrivals to map a general class of stochastic models of post-transcriptional regulation onto models that resemble promoter-based regulation. This approach leads to exact analytical results for the moments of protein distributions, and in certain cases the full distribution itself, using known exact results for mRNA distributions undergoing arbitrary promoter-based regulation. We further extend the framework to incorporate transcriptional bursting, leading to a versatile, unifying analytical framework for analyzing post-transcriptional regulation in stochastic gene expression.

more.title: Beta-Particle Transport and Thermalization in Kilonova Ejecta with Detailed Atomic Microphysics
more.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
more.abstract: When two neutron stars collide, they eject material containing heavy nuclei formed by the rapid neutron capture process (r-process). As these nuclei decay, they power a bright optical/near-infrared transient known as a kilonova (KN). Modeling KN emission is a complex problem involving atomic opacities, radiation transport, and heating powered by the thermalization of radioactive decay products like γ-rays, α-particles, and β-particles. For heating by γ-rays, many KN modeling codes do full radiation transport calculations. However, heating by α- and β-particles relies on simplified descriptions of collisions and transport, and remains an important source of uncertainty in KN models. In this paper, we study the thermalization and transport of β-particles. To study thermalization, we use evaluated atomic physics data to estimate per-species contributions to energy deposition, scattering, and electron impact ionization, which we make available online. To include non-local effects, we develop a fully relativistic framework for charged particle transport in a spherically symmetric, homologously expanding ejecta, considering two limiting magnetic-field geometries. Non-local energy deposition and escape reduce thermalization efficiency, especially in the innermost and outermost ejecta, lowering the ejecta temperature and ionization state compared to local deposition models. Coulomb scattering partially offsets these effects by trapping particles at intermediate times ∼3 − 30 days post-merger. Ionization by secondary electrons significantly enhances the overall ionization rate. We provide analytic prescriptions for the spatially dependent thermalization efficiency for use in future light-curve calculations. Our results demonstrate that evaluated atomic data and…

more.title: Set them free: extending RAMCOAL to model massive black hole triplets in hydrodynamical simulations of galaxies
more.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
more.abstract: Massive black hole binaries (MBHBs) and the higher-order multiples produced by repeated galaxy mergers evolve through regimes that cosmological simulations cannot resolve. These regimes determine merger delays, spins, recoils, and host galaxies at coalescence. We extend the RAMCOAL subgrid model to follow massive black hole triplets within hydrodynamical galaxy simulations. In the original three-stage binary model, black holes evolve as sink particles, undergo dynamical friction, and form bound binaries that harden through stellar scattering, gas torques, circumbinary-disc coupling, and gravitational-wave emission. When a hierarchical triplet becomes chaotic, RAMCOAL samples a library of outcomes from direct N-body experiments and follows the resulting mergers, exchanges, and ejections alongside the accretion and spin evolution of each black hole. Isolated-galaxy tests with different triplet geometries show that orbital configuration alone can change which pair merges and its coalescence time. For the first time, we follow an MBH triplet to coalescence within a hydrodynamical simulation of gas-rich galaxies, coupling triplet-driven mergers to host-galaxy evolution. Subgrid integration costs ≲ 1 ms of single-core time per MBH system and time step, independently of particle resolution. The resulting coalescence properties reflect the environment encountered during subgrid evolution. RAMCOAL thus provides a step towards merger catalogues linking gravitational-wave signatures to the galaxies in which the black holes evolve.

more.title: Correcting for the effects of the point spread function in intra-halo light measurements and application to deep Hyper Suprime-Cam data
more.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
more.abstract: The intra-halo light (IHL) is the diffuse stellar component that surrounds galaxies, groups, and clusters. Its formation is linked to the hierarchical assembly of the system, making it a key tracer of galaxy evolution. However, the low surface brightness of the IHL makes it challenging to detect and distinguish from the point spread function (PSF) effect of the telescope. In this paper, we present an innovative technique that corrects for PSF-scattering effects in astronomical images. We use this method to provide a statistically robust estimation of the IHL in galaxy groups and clusters by fitting an exponential model to this component using an MCMC optimiser algorithm. To test our methodology, we build 5440 mock observations of Galaxy And Mass Assembly (GAMA) groups using data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program Public Data Release 3 (HSC-SSP PDR3). Each mock contains an IHL component with a flux fraction (fIHL) ranging from 0.01 to 0.5. Our results demonstrate the importance of properly removing the PSF-scattered light, especially at lower fIHL. The IHL effective radius is overestimated by ∼9.1 and ∼2 at fIHL = 0.01 and 0.5, respectively, while the IHL flux requires correction for fIHL < 0.4, with an overestimate of ∼84.4 at fIHL = 0.01. After applying our PSF correction, the recovered flux and effective radius are much closer to their true values. Finally, we apply our methodology to HSC-PDR3 UD real observations of the GAMA group G400138 in the g,r and i-bands, finding median IHL fractions of: fg, IHL ∼ 0.19^(+0.09)_(-0.01), fr, IHL ∼ 0.08^(+0.06)_(-0.02), and fi, IHL ∼ 0.06^(+0.04)_(-0.02).

more.title: Local Pitch Angles of Galactic Structures in Nearby Galaxies with JWST: II. Dust Lanes and Gas Flows in Bar-Dominated Systems
more.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
more.abstract: We present a spatially resolved study of local pitch angles in six barred spiral galaxies observed by PHANGS–JWST, focusing on bar-dominated regions where dust lanes are the main structures. We combine a two-dimensional Fourier transform (2D-FT) with a circular-window correlation method to map pitch angles across multiple wavelengths and spatial scales, extending our previous analysis of spiral arms and interarm substructures in disk-dominated galaxies. The dust lanes show relatively large pitch angles, typically |α| ≃ 35○–70○, well above those measured for spiral arms. In several galaxies, the pitch angle changes systematically along the dust lane, with smaller values in the inner regions and larger values farther along the bar, tracing variations in local curvature. The multi-scale analysis shows that larger windows recover the overall geometry of the dust lanes, whereas smaller windows reveal local irregularities and secondary structures. MIRI images generally provide the clearest view of the dust morphology and allow a more precise characterization of local pitch-angle variations, while NIRCam offers a complementary view of the underlying stellar distribution. Unlike spiral-arm pitch angles, which are commonly associated with density-wave patterns, the values measured here characterize the local orientation and curvature of dust lanes associated with bar-driven gas flows. Together with the results of our companion study of disk-dominated galaxies, these findings support a unified, scale-dependent framework in which local pitch angles serve as observational diagnostics of distinct dynamical regimes in nearby galaxies.

more.title: Fluid eMTBR-tau243 as a Biomarker of Mixed 3-Repeat and 4-Repeat Tau Pathology

The endogenously cleaved form of tau microtubule binding region containing the residue 243 (eMTBR-tau243) can be detected in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and blood and has been associated with AD tau pathology, but its specificity and biological interpretation in non-AD tauopathies remains unclear. Objective: To evaluate biofluid eMTBR-tau243 in a range of tauopathies. Samples were analyzed between August 2023 and December 2025. Data analysis occurred from August 2024 to July 2026. Differences in biomarker levels between groups were evaluated using analysis of variance or analysis of covariance, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was calculated to evaluate the discriminative performance of fluid eMTBR-tau243. more.title: Exploring the distributional implications of targeted residential electrification in California
more.abstract: The economics of residential electrification in high-cost electricity regions remain uncertain. Using metered data from over 20,000 California homes, we assess the economic, environmental, and equity impacts of end-use electrification under rollout strategies based on household income and gas infrastructure age. Even under favorable electricity rates, only 15% of households achieve positive net present values (NPVs). Cost-effectiveness improves with deeper electrification scenarios, particularly when more costs are shifted to fixed charges and for homes with existing air conditioning—54–67% of these households break even when electrifying space heating, compared to fewer than 5% of those without. Income-based rebates more than double the share of low- and moderate-income households with positive NPVs. Prioritizing areas with aging gas infrastructure yields emissions reductions on par with high-income-led adoption and avoids costly pipeline replacement, but requires the highest subsidy to achieve cost-effectiveness across all households. These findings highlight trade-offs in designing equitable electrification strategies.

In preclinical models, 3,4,3-LI(1,2-HOPO) removed a broad range of actinides, and its oral route supports scalable emergency medical use. Objective: To evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetic parameters, and excretion of a single dose of HOPO 14-1 in healthy adults. shortlist.title: Topological Multicomponent Superconductivity with Sizable s -Wave Admixture in Twisted Bilayer Cuprates
shortlist.abstract: We investigate multicomponent superconductivity in twisted bilayer cuprates with order parameter s + d 1 e i ϕ 1 + d 2 e i ϕ 2 , where s = s 1 + s 2 is the layer-symmetric s -wave pairing and d i is the d -wave pairing in layer i . When ϕ 1 − ϕ 2 ≠ 0 , π , this three-component state spontaneously breaks time-reversal and C 4 rotational symmetries and can realize a topologically nontrivial phase. Ginzburg-Landau analysis and self-consistent mean-field calculations show that this state is stabilized over a broad parameter regime. We further identify nematic Kerr anisotropy as a key signature distinguishing it from s + i d and d 1 + e i ϕ d 2 , and find that its Josephson critical current remains sizable near the 45 ∘ twist. Our results show that s -wave pairing does not preclude chiral topological superconductivity, pointing to twisted cuprates as a more robust platform than previously appreciated.

shortlist.title: Nonperturbative constraints on stability and renormalization group flows in nonequilibrium matter
shortlist.abstract: We derive constraints on renormalization group (RG) flows and stability of phases in nonequilibrium systems using quantum information inequalities. These constraints involve conditional mutual information (CMI), which quantifies correlations between spatially separated regions not mediated by their surroundings. First, assuming CMI is UV finite, we derive a monotonicity constraint on its crossover scaling function. Under certain assumptions, this implies that the CMI scaling exponent cannot increase along the RG flow. Second, we bound the CMI of a convex mixture of states in terms of the CMI of individual components. We use this inequality to infer perturbative stability of spontaneous symmetry breaking states against quantum channels that explicitly break symmetry. We illustrate these constraints through several examples, including decoherence-driven transitions in classical symmetry-broken states, area-law CMI in anisotropic conserved dynamics, and even transitions in pure quantum states. We also discuss implications for classical nonequilibrium steady states.

shortlist.title: Odd-Parity Magnons in the Haldane-Hubbard Model from Topological Exciton Condensation
shortlist.abstract: Collective excitations in condensed matter can carry nontrivial topology and provide information about quantum phases beyond their ground-state properties. At the same time, the recent emergence of altermagnetism and related nonrelativistic spin-split electronic states raises the question of how unconventional magnetic symmetry is encoded in their collective excitations. Here, we uncover a continuous evolution from topological excitons to odd-parity magnons across an interaction-driven magnetic transition in the paradigmatic Haldane-Hubbard model. In the paramagnetic phase, our newly found sharp topological excitons soften and condense into a collinear Néel state, where they evolve into Goldstone magnons displaying characteristic f -wave spin splitting. The topology of these collective modes is tied to the underlying electronic topology, such that an electron bandgap closing enforces a magnon bandgap closing, changing the magnon topology. Our results establish a direct connection between topological collective excitations and nonrelativistic odd-parity spin splittings, with potential realizations in Floquet-driven materials and cold atomic gases.

shortlist.title: Magic without entanglement: Exact revivals and their Fisher information origin
shortlist.abstract: Magic and entanglement are independent quantum resources, yet their exact relation in many-body dynamics has remained elusive. We uncover two structural principles. First, at any stabilizer state, the curvature of the second stabilizer R'enyi entropy under an arbitrary Hermitian generator equals the quantum Fisher information up to a fixed normalization, creating a bidirectional bridge between computational and metrological resources. Second, for commuting Ising evolution on any forest graph, a Clifford pruning circuit yields the full stabilizer-R'enyi family at arbitrary size and in any spatial embedding, thereby furnishing a graph-theoretic construction of families with finite magic density and vanishing entanglement density in the thermodynamic limit. We solve two paradigmatic one-dimensional realizations central to quantum simulation—an Ising quench and a kicked Floquet chain—exactly for arbitrary system size and directly in the thermodynamic limit, revealing finite magic density with vanishing entanglement density, distinct magic and entanglement revival periods, and Clifford points with zero magic but finite bipartite entanglement. The same tangent geometry fixes initial growth and perturbative revival lifting, and a replica cluster expansion establishes the stability of thermodynamic magic minima uniformly in system size. Large scale Pauli-basis matrix-product-state calculations verify all predictions, and the tangent bridge yields a concrete protocol for detecting magic near stabilizer reference states through established quantum-Fisher-information measurements.

shortlist.title: Detection and Statistics of Large-scale Sector Boundary Crossings in the Solar Wind: The SBCross Catalog
shortlist.abstract: Heliospheric sector boundary crossings (SBCs), composed of the heliospheric current sheet (HCS), heliospheric plasma sheet (HPS), and surrounding plasma halo, represent fundamental structures in the solar wind that influence interplanetary dynamics and space weather. We present the SBCross catalog, an automated, publicly available database containing 1076 SBC events derived from in situ observations spanning more than 30 yr (1995–2026), covering Solar Cycles 23 and 24 alongside the rising and maximum phases of Solar Cycle 25. By combining interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) and 255 eV suprathermal electron pitch angle distribution (PAD) data, our algorithm reliably captures large-scale polarity transitions, with 76% of detected SBCs exhibiting clear HPS signatures ( β > 1, n peak > 10 cm −3 ). Across the catalog, we find an average occurrence rate of ≈2.6 events per Carrington rotation, a median event duration of ≈9.0 hr, and a median physical thickness of ≈7.4 × 10 6 km. Furthermore, approximately ≈15% of detected SBCs interact with interplanetary coronal mass ejections (CMEs), with this proportion rising up to 33% during solar maximum. These CME-associated events exhibit systematically longer durations (median of 10.0 hr), 54% larger physical thicknesses, and higher average solar wind velocities. Notably, all high-velocity SBC events (>600 km s −1 ) are exclusively driven by CME interactions, demonstrating local plasma pileup and structural entanglement resulting from fast CMEs overtaking the ambient slow background. The SBCross catalog serves as an updated successor to the classic SBC list by L. Svalgaard, delivering a standardized, open-access resource for the heliophysics community to systematically investigate sector boundary transitions.

shortlist.title: Are Nucleosynthetic Yields Universal? Interpreting the Multielemental Abundances of Quiescent Galaxies over Cosmic Time Using Milky Way Stars
shortlist.abstract: The detailed abundance patterns of quiescent galaxies offer powerful constraints on their formation and evolution. Yet physical insight remains elusive, as nucleosynthetic yields are notoriously uncertain. We introduce a framework that circumvents this problem by using Milky Way abundance trends as empirical proxies for initial mass function (IMF)-averaged yields. Applied to quiescent galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey ( z ∼ 0), LEGA-C ( z ∼ 0.7), and JWST/SUSPENSE ( z ∼ 2), our approach recovers the α - and Fe-peak abundances with a median offset of ∼0.05 dex across 10 elements, compared to ∼0.23 dex for theoretical yields. Systematic residuals of up to ∼0.1–0.2 dex remain for some elements in galaxies with the highest velocity dispersions. The largest discrepancies arise in N, Sr, Ba, and (at z ∼ 2) C, all of which depend on asymptotic giant branch enrichment, a channel we do not explicitly model. We explore the impact of a top-heavy IMF and find that it can shift the IMF-averaged core-collapse supernova yields by ∼0.05–0.2 dex in a direction that reduces the systematic residuals. Surprisingly, the predictions succeed without modeling the full chemical-evolution history of a galaxy: Mg and Fe alone are sufficient to predict the remaining α - and Fe-peak elements. Combined with previous results in dwarf galaxies and the Milky Way disk, this success suggests that the IMF-averaged nucleosynthetic yields of α - and Fe-peak elements are largely universal. This predictability makes the empirical yields immediately useful: embedding them in stellar population synthesis models will improve inferences on stellar populations and star formation histories, while incorporating them into cosmological simulations will produce more observationally motivated predictions.

shortlist.title: First Principles Magnetohydrodynamical Theory for the Expanding Box Model: Effects on Expansion-induced Alfvén Wave Reflection
shortlist.abstract: The expanding box model (EBM) has been widely employed to simulate multiscale plasma phenomena in the expanding solar wind by transforming the MHD equations to a comoving, noninertial frame. However, traditional formulations have suffered from historical ambiguity regarding the physical separation between the comoving and inertial reference frames, primarily arising from a classical approximation of an invariant magnetic field between them. To resolve this inconsistency, we reformulate the EBM from first principles using a fully covariant approach. Here, we model the expanding solar wind frame as an anisotropic expanding spacetime metric, allowing us to incorporate radial acceleration profiles and differential transverse expansion, ensuring that all physical fields are correctly transformed by expansion. We demonstrate that asymmetries identified in previous EBM-MHD literature are direct consequences of neglecting the tensorial scaling of the magnetic field. Our covariant treatment eliminates these residues, restoring symmetry in the comoving frame. Projecting our system back into the inertial frame clarifies the distinction between local plasma dynamics and plasma expansion, revealing the anisotropy of the Parker spiral as a geometric projection. Furthermore, linear wave analysis using Elsässer variables reveals that plasma expansion induces a low-frequency cutoff and geometric damping. Numerical integration demonstrates that expansion drives the reflection of Alfvén waves, generating counter-propagating modes primarily at low frequencies relative to the expansion rate, while high frequencies converge to the WKB approximation. This provides a consistent foundation for simulations, establishing that expansion can serve as a source of counter-propagating waves…

shortlist.title: From “KGeP” to the Protonated P4-like Anion (HGe3P)2– and the Endohedral Zintl Cluster [Mn@Ge10P2]3–
shortlist.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
shortlist.abstract: P4-like Zintl anions (Tt2Pn2)2–, which combine the properties of the formally underlying homoatomic units, Tt44– or Pn4 (Tt = tetrel, group 14 element; Pn = pnictogen, group 15 element), are versatile starting materials for ternary clusters. However, not all of the theoretically possible Tt/Pn elemental combinations are accessible, and not all of them show decent reactivity. A particularly challenging elemental combination is that of Ge and P, in contrast to homoatomic P4 or Gen4– (n = 4, 9) that are widely used for corresponding reactions. The only report on a trinuclear complex, [Cd3(Ge3P)3]3–, obtained by reacting a “(Ge2P2)2–” anion, raised questions about the assumed 2:2 ratio of the atoms in the starting material. Herein, we aimed at clarifying the mystery about the composition and identifying a means of accessing new M/Ge/P-based cluster architectures. Regarding the first, we disclosed that the anion is actually not a 2:2 unit, but the first protonated version of a binary P4-like Zintl anion, (HGe3P)2–, which finally rationalizes the composition of the previously reported trinuclear complex. The anion was obtained as its [K(crypt-222)]+ salt by the extraction of “KGeP” with ethane-1,2-diamine (en), acting as a Brønsted acid toward the Zintl anion. 1H NMR spectroscopy and computations of NMR chemical shifts confirmed the presence of the protonated anion in the salt and in solution. As (HGe3P)2– did not show the desired reactivity, we used the more reductive extraction solution of “KGeP” in situ for a follow-up reaction with [Mn(Cp*)2], yielding the first Ge/P-based endohedral Zintl cluster, [Mn@Ge10P2]3–.
